Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- A one-of-a-kind bicycle belonging to U.S. cycling legend Lance Armstrong was stolen from a team truck in California just hours after he rode it Saturday on the first day of a nine-day race. Lance Armstrong is racing in the California Amgen Tour as he attempts a comeback after retiring in 2005. Cancer survivor and seven-time Tour de France champion Armstrong is racing in the Amgen Tour of California this week as he continues his latest comeback after retiring from the sport in 2005. Armstrong's first comeback came in 1998, two years after he was diagnosed with advanced testicular cancer that had spread to his lungs and brain. Doctors gave him a less than 50 percent chance of survival. Armstrong announced the bike theft on his Twitter account Sunday morning and posted a photograph. "There is only one like it in the world therefore hard to pawn it off. Reward being offered," the Texan wrote before going out and finishing fifth in Sunday's testing first stage won by Spain's Francisco Mancebo. Swiss Olympic champion Fabian Cancellara, who started the day in the yellow jersey after winning Saturday's time-trial prologue, pulled out midway through the stage feeling unwell. Armstrong improved from 10th to fifth overall, one minute five seconds adrift, with Astana teammate Levi Leipheimer, the two-time defending champion, in second place behind Mancebo. "Holy hell. That was terrible," commented Armstrong who had a puncture. "Maybe one of the toughest days I've had on a bike, purely based on the conditions. I'm still freezing." The bicycle that was stolen is not the one that Armstrong rides every day during the race. The stolen bike is used only for time trials, a race in which cyclists ride individually at staggered intervals over a set distance and try to get the best time. The thieves took four bikes from a truck Armstrong's Astana team had parked behind a hotel in Sacramento. The other three bicycles belonged to team members Janez Brajkovic, Steve Morabito and Yaroslav Popovych, Astana said. Armstrong, 37, won the Tour de France, considered the premiere bicycle race in the world, a record seven times from 1999-2005. The 750-mile Amgen Tour of California ends Sunday. It is the second major race in which Armstrong has participated since announcing his comeback in September. He raced last month in the Tour Down Under in Australia, finishing 29th. Armstrong said he is aiming for another Tour de France victory this summer and was not expected to contend in the Australian race, which he used to gauge his fitness level after more than three years out of the saddle.

**SACRAMENTO, Calif. —** Lance Armstrong’s return to professional cycling took an unexpected turn when thieves stole his custom time-trial bicycle from an Astana team vehicle during the Tour of California, turning a piece of specialized racing equipment into the center of an international search.

“There is only one like it in the world,” Armstrong wrote at the time, emphasizing how easily the machine could be identified.

The theft added an unusual complication to one of cycling’s most closely watched comeback stories. He said the comeback would help promote cancer awareness through the Livestrong campaign he founded after surviving advanced testicular cancer.

Following surgery and chemotherapy, he returned to competition and became the sport’s dominant stage racer. Even small changes in saddle height, handlebar position or pedal setup can affect a rider’s performance.

A few days later, Sacramento police announced that the bicycle had been recovered. An unidentified person brought it to police headquarters, and authorities confirmed that it was Armstrong’s missing Trek. The circumstances surrounding its return were not immediately clear, and the investigation into the theft continued.

## Thieves Steal Lance Armstrong’s Time-Trial Bike After California Prologue

Lance Armstrong’s return to American racing took an unexpected turn when thieves stole his custom time-trial bike from the Astana team truck following the prologue of the 2009 Tour of California in Sacramento.

The Trek Equinox TTX, used by Armstrong in the opening time trial, was taken overnight from a locked team vehicle parked outside Astana’s hotel. Road bikes belonging to teammates Janez Brajkovic, Steve Morabito and Yaroslav Popovych were also reported missing.

Armstrong publicized the theft through Twitter, posting a photograph of the distinctive bike and asking for its return. Trek offered a $10,000 reward for information leading to the recovery of the bicycles.

The theft did not prevent Armstrong from continuing because Astana and Trek had replacement equipment available. Nevertheless, the missing machine was difficult to overlook: it had been specially prepared for Armstrong’s comeback and featured a unique paint scheme.

On the road, world time-trial champion Fabian Cancellara won the 3.9-kilometer Sacramento prologue. The Swiss rider completed the short course in 4 minutes, 32.9 seconds, narrowly beating defending champion Levi Leipheimer of Astana. David Zabriskie finished third.

Armstrong placed 10th, about four seconds behind Cancellara. The result left him close to the leaders in the overall standings and represented another step in his return after more than three years away from professional cycling.

The seven-time Tour de France winner had begun his comeback at Australia’s Tour Down Under before traveling to California. His schedule also included a planned debut at the Giro d’Italia in May, followed by a return to the Tour de France in July.

Armstrong’s presence at the Tour was expected to create a complicated leadership situation within Astana. Alberto Contador, the 2007 Tour champion, was already regarded as the team’s principal contender, while Leipheimer was also an established Grand Tour leader. Armstrong said his form and the race itself would help determine his role, although his return inevitably fueled speculation that he would try to win an eighth Tour.

For the moment, however, the immediate challenge was more practical: replacing stolen equipment while remaining within striking distance of Cancellara and Leipheimer in California.
